followUps:
The four WCAG principles are Perceivable, Operable, Understandable and Robust, often shortened to POUR. Each one is a question about your page.

  • Perceivable: can users sense the content? Example: alt text for images, captions for video.
  • Operable: can they use it? Example: everything works by keyboard, no timing traps.
  • Understandable: is it clear? Example: plain labels and helpful error messages.
  • Robust: does it work with assistive tech? Example: valid HTML and correct names, roles and states.

A situational limitation is a temporary condition caused by the environment, not by a disability. Example: using a phone in bright sunlight where low-contrast text vanishes, or in a noisy train where video without captions is useless.

Another is holding a baby in one arm, so you can only tap with one thumb. Designing for permanent disabilities (high contrast, captions, large touch targets) fixes these too, which is why accessibility helps everyone.

Use ARIA only when native HTML cannot express what you need. Typical cases are custom widgets with no native element (tabs, tree, combobox), live regions, and extra relationships such as aria-describedby or aria-expanded on a native button.

The first rule of ARIA is: do not use it if a native element does the job. ARIA changes only what assistive tech is told, not behaviour, so you must also add the keyboard handling and focus management yourself. Wrong ARIA is worse than none.

I always include header, nav, main and footer, so screen-reader users can jump straight to them. Use exactly one main per page.

Add aside for related content, and section or form only when given an accessible name (aria-label), because then they become landmarks. If you have two nav elements, label each ("Primary", "Footer") so users can tell them apart.

code.title: Div-as-button: Enter on keydown, Space on keyup

followUps:
Space fires on keyup because that is how a native button behaves: pressing down only arms it, and the click happens when you release. This lets a user press Space, change their mind, and move away before releasing.

Enter fires on keydown instead. Also call preventDefault() on Space keydown, otherwise the page scrolls. If you fired on Space keydown, holding the key would repeat the action, and users with tremors could trigger it by accident.

Adding role="button" changes only what assistive tech is told. It does not make the element focusable, give it a name, or make Enter and Space work. A keyboard user cannot even reach it.

You still need tabindex="0", key handlers, a visible focus style, an accessible name and disabled handling. Each missing piece is a bug the native <button> gives you for free.

An element leaves the accessibility tree when it is not rendered or is explicitly hidden. The main causes are display:none, visibility:hidden, the hidden attribute, aria-hidden="true" and inert.

Also role="presentation" or role="none" removes the element's own semantics (not its children), and purely generic wrappers like a plain div are pruned. Off-screen positioning (left:-9999px) does not remove it, which is how visually hidden text works.

display:none removes the element from rendering, the tree and the Tab order, so nobody sees or hears it. aria-hidden="true" only removes it from the accessibility tree: it is still visible, and a focusable child inside can still be reached by Tab, which creates a focus trap into silence.

So never put aria-hidden on something focusable. Use hidden or inert to hide from everyone.

code.title: Accessible name: first non-empty source wins

followUps:
The title attribute is a poor name because it is a tooltip: it appears only on mouse hover, not on keyboard focus or touch, and screen readers handle it inconsistently. It is also used as a description when another name exists.

It is only a last-resort fallback, for example for an iframe. Use visible text or a real <label> instead, so every user sees the same name that assistive tech announces.

aria-labelledby is better when the name already exists as visible text elsewhere, or when it is built from several pieces. Example: a dialog named by its heading, <h2 id="t">Delete file</h2> with aria-labelledby="t".

It stays in sync with the visible text, is easy to translate, and can point to hidden text too. aria-label is a string hidden in an attribute, so it is often forgotten when the text changes and does not get translated by some tools.

code.title: Tabs: roving tabindex and arrow keys

followUps:
Use automatic activation when the panel content is cheap and already loaded, so moving focus to a tab immediately shows its panel. It feels fast and is the simplest for screen-reader users.

Use manual activation when showing a panel is slow or costly (a network fetch, a heavy chart): arrows only move focus, and Enter or Space selects. Otherwise someone arrowing through 5 tabs would trigger 5 loads. Either way, document the behaviour and keep it consistent.

For vertical tabs, set aria-orientation="vertical" on the tablist and swap the arrow keys: Up and Down move between tabs instead of Left and Right. Home and End stay the same.

Everything else (roving tabindex, aria-selected, aria-controls, wrapping) is unchanged. Horizontal tabs use aria-orientation="horizontal", which is the default for a tablist.

code.title: Modal focus trap with wrap-around and focus return

followUps:
Focus is lost: the browser moves it to the body, so keyboard and screen-reader users start again from the top of the page. That is disorienting after a long page.

Plan a fallback: before closing, check opener.isConnected. If it was removed, focus a sensible nearby element, such as the next item in a list, the list heading, or the main heading. Never leave focus on a removed element or on body.

aria-hidden on siblings only hides them from screen readers. Keyboard users can still Tab into the hidden page and mouse users can still click it, so you need extra code and it is easy to miss one element.

inert removes the whole subtree from the tab order, pointer events, text selection and the accessibility tree in one attribute. The native <dialog>.showModal() does this for you automatically.

code.title: WCAG contrast ratio and AA/AAA verdicts

followUps:
Because #767676 is the lightest grey that still passes AA on white: its ratio is about 4.54:1, just above 4.5. One step lighter, #777777, gives 4.48:1 and fails.

It is a handy default for secondary text on white backgrounds. The program above prints both numbers so you can see the cliff. Remember it only passes on white; on an off-white or tinted background it may fail.

APCA (Accessible Perceptual Contrast Algorithm) is a newer way to measure contrast. It accounts for text size, weight, and polarity (dark on light vs light on dark), and gives a score called Lc instead of a ratio. It models human vision better than the old WCAG 2 formula.

It is not a legal standard. WCAG 2.x ratios (4.5:1, 3:1) are what laws and audits use. APCA was proposed for WCAG 3, which is still a draft, so use it as a design aid, not a compliance test.

A placeholder disappears as soon as you type, so users must remember what the field wanted. It also usually has low contrast, is not always announced as the name, and is not translated or zoomed reliably.

It hurts people with memory or attention difficulties the most. Use a visible <label> that stays on screen, and keep the placeholder only for an example format such as "name@example.com".

WCAG 3.3.7 (Redundant Entry) says do not make users type the same information twice in one process: auto-fill it or let them select it. Example: a "shipping address same as billing" checkbox.

WCAG 3.3.8 (Accessible Authentication, minimum) says login must not depend on a cognitive test such as remembering a password or solving a puzzle, unless there is an alternative. In practice: allow paste and password managers, and offer email links or passkeys.

code.title: Toast announcer: dedupe, queue, clear before write

followUps:
It stays silent because the live region was created at the same moment as its content. Screen readers watch an existing region for changes; a brand-new node is just added, not changed, so many do not announce it.

Fix: render an empty role="alert" or aria-live container when the app starts, and later set its text. role="alert" inserted together with text works in some browsers, but not reliably, so do not depend on it.

Assertive interrupts whatever the screen reader is saying, so use it only when waiting would cause harm: a session about to expire in 30 seconds, a payment failure, or a form submission error that blocks progress.

Use polite for everything else ("Saved", "3 results found"), because it waits until the user is idle. Overusing assertive makes users miss what they were reading, so most toasts should be polite.

Automated tools like axe catch only about 30 to 40 percent of issues, because many problems need human judgement. Axe cannot tell if alt text is accurate, whether the reading order makes sense, or whether a keyboard flow is usable.

It also cannot judge if a label is meaningful ("Click here"), whether focus moves to a sensible place after an action, whether content is understandable, or how a real screen reader sounds. That is why a manual checklist and screen-reader testing are still needed.

First report the defects to the vendor and check for a more accessible version or alternative product. Meanwhile, wrap the widget with a safer experience: an accessible fallback (a native form or link), a clear label and a visible focus ring around it.

Add the problem to your risk log and contract requirements (ask for a VPAT or conformance report). In future choices, test widgets before buying. If it cannot be fixed, replace it; do not hide it with an overlay.

They help by default only a little. A framework gives you the router, but you still handle accessibility yourself. Next.js App Router includes a route announcer, a visually hidden live region that reads the new page title, and React Router offers hooks and ScrollRestoration.

You should still set a unique document.title per route and move focus to the new h1 (with tabindex="-1"). Test with a screen reader, because the built-in announcement is not always enough.

A virtualised list renders only about 20 of 10,000 rows, so assistive tech sees only those. Set aria-setsize (total, 10000) and aria-posinset (this row's index) on each item so users know their position.

Keep focus on a stable element when rows are recycled, support keyboard navigation (arrows, Home, End, PageUp, PageDown), and offer search or a "jump to" control. Keep the focused row rendered even when it scrolls out of view.

I explain the problem to the designer and propose an alternative with the same goal, backed by a quick prototype, rather than quietly shipping something inaccessible. Example: a hover-only menu becomes a click-to-open button, and a 2.5:1 grey text becomes 4.5:1.

If a business decision still overrides it, I document the exception, the affected users and the risk, and get sign-off. The earlier designers and developers review designs together, the less this happens.

Treat an accessibility fix as a bug fix where possible and release it as a patch, following semver. Keep the component's props and DOM structure the same so that consumer CSS and tests do not break.

If a fix changes behaviour (for example, a new keyboard map or a DOM change), release it as a minor with a changelog entry, or as a major with a codemod. Use feature flags for risky changes, and provide a short migration note for each release.

Give the assistant a specific job and checklist, and ask for evidence. Example prompt: "Review this component for accessibility. Check semantic elements, accessible names, keyboard operation, focus management, ARIA validity, contrast, and reduced motion. List each issue with the line and a fix."

Provide the code and the intended behaviour. Then verify its answer yourself with axe and a keyboard run, because the assistant can hallucinate wrong ARIA attributes or claim it passes.

Overlays are scripts that claim to make a site compliant with one line of JavaScript. They draw criticism because they cannot fix real structural problems such as wrong markup, missing labels or broken keyboard flows, and they often interfere with the screen readers users already have.

Many users find them intrusive, they give a false sense of compliance, and some companies using them were still sued. The accessible fix is to correct the underlying code, not to patch it on top.
